data.text/html:
Survival analysis: how long until it happens?

An interactive companion to two videos: DataMListic, "Survival Analysis - Explained" (a subscription app asking "how long does a user stay?") and Biostatistics, "Mini Lecture: Survival Analysis" (a cancer trial asking "does the new treatment help people survive longer?"). Both videos tell the same story with different examples. Some of your stories haven't ended yet, and the whole field exists to use those unfinished stories without throwing them away or making up their endings.

data.text/markdown:
Color language used throughout
color meaning
■ orange-red an event: a cancellation or a death (we saw it happen)
■ blue censored: still going when we stopped watching (we only know "at least this long")
■ purple the Kaplan-Meier estimate ||(\hat S(t)||)
■ dashed grey the true curve (only available when we simulate)
■ amber naive answers that ignore censoring
Roadmap: 1. Censoring and the two wrong answers → 2. Survival, density and hazard → 3. Kaplan-Meier step by step →
  1. Checking against the truth (and when it breaks) → 5. What the hazard's shape tells you → 6. Comparing groups with the log-rank test → sandbox, quiz, recap. The Cox proportional hazards model gets only a teaser here; it has its own notebook, cox_proportional_hazards.py.

1 · Censoring: the stories that haven't ended

The app. Your manager asks "how long does a user stay before they cancel?". You pull up eight users. Four of them canceled (●, orange-red). Four are still subscribed (○ with a dashed arrow, blue). One of them only joined 3 months ago. Their missing endings are what statisticians call censoring. The trial. It's the same problem in the cancer study. You can't run a study until everyone has died, so it stops at a fixed date. Patients still alive at the end, plus the [often 30%+] who drop out for reasons like travel, work or moving house, are right-censored. We know their event lies somewhere to the right of the last time we saw them. Two tempting fixes, both too low:
  1. Drop the active users and take the median of the people who left. But the loyal 9-month user is exactly who you threw out.
  2. Pretend the active users cancel today. This invents a cancellation that never happened.
Instead, use what a censored user really tells us: "my stay is at least this long." Drag a bar's end to change its length. Click an end marker to switch between canceled and still active.

data.text/markdown:
Not just right-censoring: the Mini Lecture's other ways to have incomplete stories

phenomenon what we know example from the lecture
Right-censored the event is after the last time we looked still alive at study end; dropped out; GFP signal above the detection limit; too many bacteria to count
Left-censored the event happened before some time, but we don't know how long before infection first seen at a positive test; the egg is already there in the morning
Interval-censored only that the event fell between two times infected during a holiday, tested afterwards; COVID infection between exposure and positive test
Left-truncated people who had the event before entry never appear delayed entry into the trial: you had to survive long enough to be diagnosed
Right-truncated only people who already had the event appear historical death records: you must have died to be in the data
Competing risk a different event happened at a known time and prevents ours a cancer patient dies in a traffic accident (handled with multi-state models)
Censored values come with a bound. Truncated units are not in the data at all. Neither is the same as ordinary missing data, where the row exists but a value is blank. Right-censoring and left-truncation are the most common. The rest of this notebook deals with right-censoring.

2 · The survival curve, the density and the hazard

DataMListic's first move is to stop chasing a single number. Let ||(T||) be the length of a stay. Then ||[S(t) = P(T > t)||]is the share still subscribed (or alive) at time ||(t||). It starts at 1 and can only go down. The median is where it crosses ½. People quote the median rather than the mean because the curve often stops before reaching 0, and the mean would need the part we never saw. Why a curve and not a histogram? A histogram needs a stay to be finished before it can go in a bin. ||(S(t)||) only asks "did you make it past ||(t||)?", and an active user can answer that for every ||(t||) up to today. Three views of one distribution:
formula reads as
density ||(f(t)||) when do events happen, overall?
survival ||(S(t) = 1-F(t)=\int_t^\infty f||) who is still here?
hazard ||(h(t) = \dfrac{f(t)}{S(t)}||) the risk of leaving right now, given you've lasted this long
The hazard is the continuous-time version of the ||(d/n||) that Kaplan-Meier multiplies (section 3). For a tiny step, ||(1-x \approx e^{-x}||), so a long product of one-step survivals becomes a sum of hazards in an exponent: ||[S(t) = \prod (1 - h\,\Delta t) \;\longrightarrow\; S(t) = \exp\!\Big(-\int_0^t h(u)\,du\Big).||]With a constant hazard ||(\lambda||) you get ||(S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}||), the exponential distribution. The Weibull with shape ||(k||) has ||(h(t) = \frac{k}{\lambda}\big(\frac{t}{\lambda}\big)^{k-1}||): falling if ||(k<1||), constant at ||(k=1||), rising (wear-out) if ||(k>1||).

Where does the e come from? Take a constant hazard of 0.3 per month. Chop each month into ||(m||) slices and survive each slice with probability ||(1-0.3/m||). As ||(m||) grows, the product of many factors close to 1 turns into ||(e^{-0.3t}||).

data.text/markdown:
3 · Kaplan-Meier, one month at a time

Surviving past month 8 means surviving month 1, then month 2 given you made it through month 1, and so on. That is just the chain rule of conditional probability. At every time ||(t_i||) with at least one event:
  • ||(n_i||) = the risk set: everyone still here and still observed,
  • ||(d_i||) = how many have the event at ||(t_i||),
||[\hat S(t) = \prod_{t_i \le t}\left(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\right).||]A censored person counts as a survivor in every step up to when we stopped seeing them, then leaves the denominators. As the Mini Lecture puts it: "the only thing that changes with censored observations is the number at risk." The censoring is drawn as a small tick, not a drop. The stepper below replays the eight users from section 1, so edit them up there and the replay follows.

data.text/markdown:
4 · Checking it against the truth (and how to break it)

Eight users can't prove anything, so DataMListic simulates a thousand. Each stay comes from a Weibull distribution with a true median of 8.3 months (a falling hazard, ||(k = 0.8||)). Users sign up at random times during a two-year study, so many are still active when it ends. In the video, dropping the actives gives 2.9 months, "cancel today" gives 4.8, and Kaplan-Meier lands at 8.5, right on top of the truth. The hidden condition: non-informative censoring. KM works if being observed tells you nothing about when someone will cancel. Here censoring depends only on the sign-up date, so the condition holds. But if users who are about to leave stop opening the app and you lose track of them early, the risk set keeps the loyal ones and the curve overestimates how long people stay. The shaded band is a 95% confidence interval from Greenwood's standard error, the uncertainty the Mini Lecture mentions.

The curve simply stops early, and the band widens at the end where few users are at risk. KM won't extrapolate.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eTurn on \u003cstrong\u003einformative censoring\u003c/strong\u003e. Now the purple curve floats \u003cstrong\u003eabove\u003c/strong\u003e the truth: the leavers vanished as \"censored\", so the risk set is full of loyal users.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eDrop \u003cstrong\u003eusers to 50\u003c/strong\u003e and watch the Greenwood band grow. Uncertainty is part of the answer.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"warn"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
5 · What the shape of the hazard tells you (and what it doesn't)

DataMListic finds the hazard shape more revealing than the survival curve: rising means wear-out, falling means early churn, and a bathtub is high, then flat, then rising again. But be careful reading a falling hazard as "users get more loyal over time." Their example: 40% of users are flaky with a 30% chance of leaving each month, and the rest are loyal at 3%. Every individual's risk is constant, month after month, yet the group's hazard falls from about 14% toward 3%, because the flaky users leave first: ||[h_{\text{pop}}(t) = \frac{p\,q_f(1-q_f)^{t-1} + (1-p)\,q_\ell(1-q_\ell)^{t-1}}{p(1-q_f)^{t-1} + (1-p)(1-q_\ell)^{t-1}}||]The hazard describes whoever is still in the risk set at that moment.

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eTry this\u003c/strong\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eAt the defaults, month 1 is ≈ 13.8% (0.4·30% + 0.6·3%), and it slides down toward 3% as the grey area empties.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet the \u003cstrong\u003etwo hazards equal\u003c/strong\u003e. The population hazard goes flat, and the \"loyalty\" illusion disappears.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSet \u003cstrong\u003ep = 0\u003c/strong\u003e or \u003cstrong\u003ep = 1\u003c/strong\u003e: a single homogeneous group has a constant hazard.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"info"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
6 · Comparing two groups: the log-rank test

Now there are two curves: women vs men in a lung-cancer cohort (the Mini Lecture's example) or annual vs monthly subscribers (DataMListic's example). Is the gap real or just noise? The log-rank test walks through every event time ||(t_j||). If the groups had the same survival, then the ||(d_j||) events would be split in proportion to who's at risk. Group 1's expected share is ||[E_{1j} = d_j \frac{n_{1j}}{n_j}, \qquad V_j = d_j\frac{n_{1j}}{n_j}\Big(1-\frac{n_{1j}}{n_j}\Big)\frac{n_j-d_j}{n_j-1}||]and we compare it with the observed ||(O_{1j}||), summed over time: ||[\chi^2 = \frac{\big(\sum_j O_{1j} - \sum_j E_{1j}\big)^2}{\sum_j V_j} \;\sim\; \chi^2_1 \text{ under } H_0.||]The lung data is the classic NCCTG lung dataset from R's survival package, the package the Mini Lecture recommends. It has 228 patients, with time in days, and loads from a public Rdatasets mirror.
Loaded 228 lung-cancer patients, 165 deaths, 90 women.

The log-rank χ² ≈ 10.3, p ≈ 0.001, the same as R's \u003ccode\u003esurvdiff\u003c/code\u003e.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eSimulation:\u003c/strong\u003e set the hazard ratio to \u003cstrong\u003e1.0\u003c/strong\u003e. data.text/markdown:
7 · Sandbox: paint a hazard, watch everything else follow

Paint the monthly hazard ||(h_t||), the chance of leaving during month ||(t||) given you were still here at its start. The purple line is the survival curve it implies, ||(S(t)=\prod_{u\le t}(1-h_u)||), computed live in your browser. When you release the mouse, Python simulates a cohort with your hazard, censors it with a study window, and checks Kaplan-Meier against the truth.
